n: A prophecy against Tyre, the great Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast (modern Lebanon), the hub of ancient sea trade. Sailors on the great trading ships hear in Cyprus that their home port is destroyed.

f.g: Large ocean-going merchant ships.
Kittim — Cyprus.

n: Be silent, people of the coast, enriched by the merchants of Sidon who sailed the seas.

f.g: Sidon, Tyre’s sister city to the north.
Coastland; Tyre was partly built on an island.

n: Across the great waters came grain from the Nile, the harvest of Egypt. Tyre grew rich trading it and became the marketplace of nations.

f.g: A branch of the Nile, or the Nile itself.
Market, trading center.

n: Sidon is shamed, for the sea itself mourns as though childless — it no longer raises sons and daughters. The sea-based trading empire has lost its people.

f.g: I have not been in labor — I am bereaved.

n: When news of Tyre’s fall reaches Egypt, Egyptians will be in anguish, since much of their trade went through Tyre.
Flee to Tarshish, the farthest port! Wail, you people of the coast!

f.g: A distant port in the west, possibly in Spain.

n: Is this your celebrated city, so ancient? Now its people will wander as exiles to distant lands.

f.w: whose antiquity is of ancient days
f.g: Tyre was very old, founded perhaps before 2000 BC.
Live as a foreigner.

n: Who planned this against Tyre, the city that crowned kings, whose merchants were princes and whose traders were honored worldwide?

f.g: The city that set up kings in its colonies.
Traders.

n: The Lord of hosts planned it, to humble all pride and bring down the honored of the earth. Wealth and fame cannot shield anyone from God.

f.w: to stain the pride of all glory

n: Colonists of Tarshish are now free to spread through their land like the Nile, for Tyre’s controlling power is gone.

f.g: No more harbor or restraint.

n: The Lord stretched His hand over the sea and shook kingdoms. He commanded the destruction of the strongholds of Canaan’s merchant city.

f.g: Literally “Canaan” — the Phoenicians were Canaanites, and the word came to mean “trader.”

n: Tyre and Sidon, once proud and untouched, will no longer celebrate. Even if they flee to Cyprus, they will find no rest.

f.g: Once-unconquered city now crushed.

n: Look at the land of the Chaldeans (Babylonia): Assyria turned it into a wilderness, built siege towers, and ruined its palaces. If Babylon could fall, so can Tyre.

f.g: Babylonia; Assyria’s Sennacherib devastated Babylon in 689 BC.

n: Wail, great trading ships, for your fortress harbor is destroyed! The chapter’s opening cry is repeated.
Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years — a normal lifespan — then will return to its trade like a forgotten prostitute singing to win back customers.

f.g: A lifetime; compare Psalms 90:10 and Jeremiah 25:11.
A picture of trading purely for profit.

n: A mocking song: “Take your harp, forgotten one, walk the city, and sing sweetly so people remember you.”
After seventy years the Lord will restore Tyre, and it will return to doing business with every kingdom on earth.

f.g: Here, restore or take notice of.
Wages, earnings.

n: But in the end, Tyre’s profits will be set apart as holy to the Lord — used to feed and clothe His people. Wealth once used selfishly will be consecrated to God.

f.g: Fine, lasting clothes.
